after: ## Comparing an LIC and an HIC (7.1.4)
alt: Two schematic population pyramids. The typical LIC pyramid is triangular, with a wide base of young dependants that narrows quickly and few elderly. The typical HIC pyramid is a column with a narrow base, straight sides and a wide top, with more women than men in the oldest group.
caption: Wide base and narrow top for an LIC; straight sides and a wide top for an HIC.

alt: A bar of rising income per person divided into low-income, middle-income (split into lower-middle and upper-middle) and high-income countries. Notes say the limits change every year and that a national average hides differences within a country.
caption: Three groups by income per person; the limits change each year.

alt: Two invented regions. Upland North has 2,400,000 people on 60,000 km², 40 people per km², shown as a sparsely dotted square. Coastal South has 900,000 people on 1,500 km², 600 people per km², shown as a densely dotted square: 15 times as dense despite fewer people.
caption: Density = population ÷ area: fewer people can still mean far more crowding.

alt: Two stacked bars of population by age. Country X: 42% aged 0 to 14, 55% aged 15 to 64 and 3% aged 65 and over, giving 81.8 dependants per 100 workers. Country Y: 15%, 64% and 21%, giving 56.3. X is the LIC with mostly young dependants; Y is the HIC with mostly elderly dependants.
caption: Same idea, opposite pressures: young dependants in the LIC, elderly in the HIC.
